title: Clinic staff lose roughly 13 hours per physician per week to prior authorization, including long holds for peer-to-peer reviews
affected_user: Front-desk staff, nurses, medical assistants, and physicians/NPs at small and mid-size outpatient practices (and the dedicated PA staff that 40% of practices now employ)
job_to_be_done: Get an insurer's approval for a prescribed drug, imaging study, or procedure quickly enough that the patient does not abandon or delay treatment
current_process: Staff look up each payer's rules, assemble documentation from the EHR, submit via payer portal, fax, or phone, then chase status; on denial, a clinician must request a peer-to-peer call inside a short window (often 24-48 hours or 7 business days) and sit on hold to reach a reviewer
what_fails: Requests are delayed or denied for missing documentation or inconsistent criteria; peer-to-peer calls require 40+ minute holds; 95% of physicians say PA delays necessary care and 79% report patients abandoning treatment
failure_frequency: ~40 PA requests per physician per week consuming ~13 hours of physician/staff time (AMA survey fielded Dec 2025, published 2026); an NP reports 2-3 hours per day on PA work (Medscape 2026)
cost_of_failure: ~13 staff/physician hours per physician per week (AMA); 40% of practices employ staff working exclusively on PA (AMA); treatment abandonment reported by 79% of physicians
existing_workaround: Hiring dedicated PA coordinators, outsourcing to billing companies, keeping per-payer cheat sheets, scheduling clinician time blocks for peer-to-peer holds, writing appeals from templates
who_pays_today: Practices (staff salaries, outsourced PA/billing vendors); patients (delayed or abandoned care); payers (reviewer and vendor costs)

sources.note: Summarizes AMA survey of 1,000 physicians (fielded Dec 2025): ~40 PAs/week, 13 hours/week, 95% say PA delays care, 79% report treatment abandonment, only one-third believe insurer pledge will help.
AMA's own write-up of its PA time-burden survey series (earlier years reported 37-45 requests/week, ~14 hours).
Nurse practitioner describes being stuck on hold with an insurer and PA work consuming 2-3 hours a day.
Physician describes repeatedly waiting on hold 40+ minutes for peer-to-peer reviewers and short windows to connect.
Explains CMS-0057-F timelines in force since Jan 1, 2026 (7 days standard, 72 hours expedited) for MA, Medicaid/CHIP, and exchange plans only; commercial plans set their own.

firsthand_evidence: A nurse practitioner told Medscape she lost part of an afternoon on hold with an insurer and that prior-auth work including peer-to-peer calls can eat 2-3 hours of her day; a physician writing in STAT described waiting on hold more than 40 minutes several times just to reach a peer reviewer.
key_unknowns: Which payers and which service lines generate the most wasted hours per request; how much of the 13 hours is status-chasing versus documentation assembly; whether the Jan 2026 CMS-0057-F decision deadlines are actually being met by MA/Medicaid plans (no 2026 compliance data found); no Reddit-level firsthand threads surfaced in search.
technical_unlock: CMS-0057-F forces impacted payers to expose FHIR Prior Authorization APIs (Da Vinci PAS/CRD/DTR) by Jan 1, 2027, with public PA metrics already due from March 2026; machine-readable payer criteria plus EHR document extraction could let a small practice auto-assemble submissions and track status without portal babysitting.
why_now: CMS-0057-F operational deadlines took effect Jan 1, 2026 and payer API deadlines hit Jan 1, 2027; insurers' June 2025 reform pledge is viewed skeptically by two-thirds of physicians; CMS's 'Axe the Fax' push targets the roughly half of PA traffic still sent by fax.
existing_solutions: Payer portals, Availity, CoverMyMeds (drug PA), EHR-embedded PA modules (Epic, athena), AI PA startups (e.g., Cohere, Rhyme, Insight Health, Muni, CareRoute per search results), outsourced billing firms.

title: WISeR prior authorization pilot in traditional Medicare is producing denials, 90-minute holds, and approvals that MACs will not pay
affected_user: Physicians and billing staff in the six WISeR states (NJ, OH, OK, TX, AZ, WA) delivering the targeted services (pain procedures, skin substitutes, nerve stimulators, etc.) to traditional Medicare patients
job_to_be_done: Obtain a WISeR vendor authorization for a covered Medicare service and then actually get paid by the Medicare Administrative Contractor for it
current_process: Submit documentation to the CMS-contracted vendor portal for the state, wait for AI-assisted plus clinician review, request peer-to-peer on denial, then bill the MAC with the vendor's authorization number
what_fails: Extended authorization timelines, vendor portal access problems, and authorization numbers issued by vendors that MACs did not accept, leaving practices unpaid despite valid approvals; pain specialists report far more denials than under commercial or MA plans; staff on hold up to 90 minutes to schedule peer-to-peer
failure_frequency: unknown (Washington Post/WP Intelligence analysis reports delays and dissatisfaction across all six states; no CMS denial-rate data found)
cost_of_failure: Unpaid claims for already-delivered services (WSMA reports practices unable to receive payment despite approvals); staff time on 90-minute holds; delayed procedures for Medicare patients
existing_workaround: Escalation through state medical associations to CMS; ASA/AOA coalition lobbying for default-approval on missed timelines and gold-card exemptions; some practices limiting WISeR-targeted services
who_pays_today: Practices (unreimbursed care, staff time); Medicare beneficiaries (delayed care); CMS pays vendors, reportedly on a share of denied-claim savings

sources.note: Summarizes WP Intelligence (Washington Post) analysis finding delays, provider dissatisfaction, long peer-to-peer waits, and vendor PA numbers not accepted by MACs across six states.
Washington State Medical Association reports extended timelines, vendor portal access difficulty, and unresolved discrepancies leaving practices unpaid despite valid approvals.
Arizona pain physician reports far more denials under WISeR than under commercial/MA and staff holding up to 90 minutes to schedule peer-to-peer.
ASA asks CMS to enforce review timelines with penalties, default to approval when missed, decouple vendor pay from denials, and create gold-card exemptions; CMS plans gold-carding from July.
Regulatory Relief Coalition argues vendor compensation tied to denial volume creates perverse incentives.

firsthand_evidence: An Arizona pain specialist told the Washington Post (relayed by the Arizona Medical Association) that his practice sees far more denials under Medicare WISeR than it ever saw from commercial insurers or Medicare Advantage, and that his staff sit on hold up to 90 minutes just to schedule a peer-to-peer review; WSMA says member practices have valid approvals the MAC will not pay.
key_unknowns: Actual WISeR denial and overturn rates (CMS has not published); how many claims are stuck in the vendor-number/MAC mismatch; whether the July 2026 gold-card exemption has reduced volume; whether the model expands beyond six states in 2027.
technical_unlock: Not primarily technical; the payment mismatch is a CMS/MAC data-integration failure. A tool that tracks each WISeR submission, authorization number, MAC claim status, and timeline-breach evidence could support appeals and association complaints, but cannot fix the underlying model.
why_now: WISeR launched Jan 2026 (first PA in traditional Medicare), Arizona law banning AI-driven claim denials took effect June 30, 2026, and CMS began gold-card exemptions in July 2026, so the rules are still shifting.
existing_solutions: State medical association advocacy, ASA/AOA coalition, existing PA vendors adding WISeR workflows; no dedicated tooling found.

title: No Surprises Act IDR volume is 20x higher than projected, with ineligible filings and delayed or absent payment after awards
affected_user: Billing managers at out-of-network emergency, anesthesia, radiology, and air-ambulance groups (and their revenue-cycle vendors); also plan staff and the certified IDR entities
job_to_be_done: Get paid a fair amount for an out-of-network emergency or ancillary service by moving a disputed claim through open negotiation and federal IDR, then collecting the award
current_process: Send 30-day open negotiation notice, file in the federal IDR portal, pay administrative and entity fees, submit offers and supporting data, wait for eligibility review and determination, then chase the payer for the awarded amount within 30 days
what_fails: Disputes are filed when ineligible (wrong jurisdiction, state law applies, batching errors), entity rationales are unclear, and payers delay or skip payment after determinations; backlog reached 430,000 outstanding disputes in mid-2025 before closures caught up
failure_frequency: Over 5.1 million dispute initiations April 2022-January 2026 vs. ~17,000/year projected (Claritev/Health Affairs); ~516,000 initiations in Dec 2025-Jan 2026 alone (CMS); 20-fold volume increase 2023Q1 to 2025Q4 (Harvard)
cost_of_failure: unknown in aggregate; each dispute carries non-refundable administrative fees plus entity fees, staff time, and months of delayed cash on awarded amounts (CMS Oct 2026 readout cites delayed payment or nonpayment after determinations)
existing_workaround: Outsourcing to IDR-management vendors and law firms, spreadsheet tracking of negotiation deadlines, batching claims, abandoning small-dollar disputes, complaints to CMS enforcement
who_pays_today: Provider groups (fees, staff, vendors taking a percentage); payers (fees, staff); CMS (IDR operations, backlog-clearing initiatives)

sources.note: CMS convening readout: users raise concerns about ineligible disputes, unclear IDR entity determination rationales, and delayed payment or nonpayment after determinations.
Harvard analysis of CMS public use files: IDR dispute volume increased 20-fold from 2023Q1 to 2025Q4.
CMS supplemental data: 257,724 disputes closed Jan 2026; Dec 2025-Jan 2026 closures (506,242) nearly equal initiations (516,241); 92% of all disputes resolved.
Health Affairs: officials expected ~17,000 disputes per year; 4.8 million total cases through end of 2025.
Georgetown CHIR: 430,000 disputes still outstanding as of late June 2025.
CMS fact sheet on initiative to clear the IDR backlog.

firsthand_evidence: CMS's own Oct 1, 2026 readout of its convening with certified IDR entities records that process users complain about disputes being filed when ineligible, determination rationales they cannot interpret, and payers paying late or not at all after an award.
key_unknowns: Share of awards unpaid or paid late (no public figure); ineligibility rate in 2026; how concentrated filing is among a few large groups/vendors (Harvard study on filer type likely answers this but detail not in snippets); whether CMS's planned fee or process changes in 2026-2027 reduce volume.
technical_unlock: CMS publishes quarterly IDR public use files and the portal has structured deadlines; a deadline-and-eligibility tracker that checks state-vs-federal jurisdiction, batching rules, and post-award payment timing against the PUF benchmarks is feasible without privileged access.
why_now: Volume tripled over 2024-2025, CMS cleared most of the backlog by Jan 2026 (so throughput is now high), and the Oct 2026 CMS convening signals process changes focused on eligibility and post-award payment.
existing_solutions: IDR-management vendors (e.g., HaloMD per search results), Claritev/MultiPlan analytics, law firms, CMS federal IDR portal.

title: New clinicians cannot bill for 90-150+ days because payer credentialing and enrollment stall on CAQH and data-mismatch errors
affected_user: Practice administrators and office managers at independent physician practices and behavioral-health group practices onboarding a new physician, NP, or therapist; solo therapists trying to join insurance panels
job_to_be_done: Get a newly hired or newly licensed clinician enrolled and in-network with each commercial payer, Medicare, and Medicaid so their visits can be billed
current_process: Build and attest a CAQH ProView profile, submit separate applications per payer (often 8-15), supply malpractice certificate, work history, licenses, and locations, then wait for monthly credentialing committee meetings and follow up by phone/email with provider relations
what_fails: Applications stall on an outdated or un-reattested CAQH profile, practice locations that do not match across CAQH/NPI/payer forms, expired malpractice certificates, and payer committees that meet only monthly; commercial timelines run 90-150 days and sometimes 180; therapists see 60-180 days per panel
failure_frequency: Every new hire, every payer; multiple vendor sources say delays past 90 days are routine in 2026 (KevinMD May 2026; getpracticehelp; medcloudmd); re-attestation needed quarterly and recredentialing every 2-3 years
cost_of_failure: Weeks to months of unbillable clinician time per hire; vendor-claimed figures of $7,500/day lost revenue and $50k-$150k per delayed provider could not be verified and should be treated as marketing
existing_workaround: Starting applications months before start date, billing under supervising provider or out-of-network while waiting, hiring credentialing specialists or outsourcing to credentialing services, spreadsheets tracking per-payer status and re-attestation dates
who_pays_today: Practices (credentialing staff, outsourced credentialing vendors charging per payer, lost revenue); new clinicians (delayed productivity bonuses); patients (fewer in-network therapists)

sources.note: Physician-facing piece on why credentialing routinely exceeds 90 days (CAQH profile staleness, mismatched locations, expired documents).
Vendor explainer: credentialing takes 90-150 days; missed CAQH re-attestation can stall an application 60 days in; payers expect attestations current within 90-120 days.
Vendor piece claiming 2026 delays often run 3-6 months; its 85% CAQH-cause figure is unsourced.
Lists the top CAQH-related failure causes (outdated profile, attestation lapses, document expiry).
Therapist paneling guide: 60-120 days per payer typical, up to six months; payers review only at monthly committee meetings; quarterly CAQH re-attestation.
Explains why a new physician cannot bill for ~90 days after hire.

firsthand_evidence: No firsthand administrator or therapist thread surfaced in search (Reddit results did not appear); the consistent 90-150 day timeline and CAQH re-attestation failure mode is reported across six independent vendor/industry sources, and KevinMD's May 2026 piece is physician-authored.
key_unknowns: Primary statistics on median enrollment time by payer in 2026 (no MGMA/CAQH data surfaced); how much of the delay is practice-side error vs. payer committee cadence; whether CAQH's own tooling has improved; Medicare PECOS/MAC processing times in 2026 (search budget exhausted before this could be checked).
technical_unlock: CAQH ProView and NPPES are structured data sources; a pre-submission consistency checker (locations, dates, expirations across CAQH/NPI/state license/malpractice) plus re-attestation and recredentialing deadline tracking is buildable by a solo developer with Playwright and public registries, without payer API access.
why_now: Practices are hiring more NPs/PAs and behavioral-health clinicians; more therapists are moving from cash-pay to panels via aggregators; no structural change found in 2026 credentialing rules, so this is a persistent rather than newly emerging pain.
existing_solutions: CAQH ProView, Medallion, Verifiable, symplr, Headway/Alma (therapist paneling aggregators), many small credentialing-service firms (per search results: DrCredentialing, CodeCure, Medicotech, etc.).

title: Six-month Medicaid renewals and work-requirement reporting under the 2025 reconciliation law will double paperwork and procedurally disenroll eligible patients
affected_user: Medicaid expansion adults (and mixed-eligibility households); eligibility workers and IT teams at state Medicaid agencies; FQHC/community health center enrollment assisters and front desks who absorb the uninsured patients
job_to_be_done: Keep an eligible person continuously covered by completing renewal and work/community-engagement documentation on time, and keep provider revenue from turning into uncompensated care
current_process: Annual ex parte or form-based renewal; starting Dec 31, 2026 expansion adults must renew every six months, and by Jan 2027 states must verify work/community engagement or exemptions (including a narrowed medical-frailty exemption under the June 1, 2026 interim final rule)
what_fails: People lose coverage for paperwork reasons rather than ineligibility (procedural disenrollment was 96% of disenrollments in New Mexico during unwinding, 80%+ in Arkansas); states must rework and reprogram IT systems; nearly two-thirds of enrollees did not know disenrollment had begun (KFF)
failure_frequency: Urban Institute: six-month redeterminations could reduce average monthly expansion enrollment by up to 3.1 million, ~11% of redetermination failures procedural; CBO: ~700,000 more uninsured in 2034 from this provision alone; New Mexico projects ~88,000 people removed by work requirements
cost_of_failure: New Mexico estimated $32.7 million initial IT cost (Aug 2025); CBO $63 billion federal spending reduction over 10 years from six-month renewals; providers absorb uncompensated care for churned patients (no FQHC-specific 2026 figure found)
existing_workaround: States choosing between all-at-once vs. rolling transition to six-month cycles (CMS March 2026 options); health centers and navigators running outreach, text reminders, and in-person renewal help; software vendors pitching churn-prevention to home-care and behavioral-health agencies
who_pays_today: States (IT reprogramming, eligibility staff, call centers); CMS; FQHCs and hospitals (uncompensated care, enrollment assisters funded by HRSA/Navigator grants); patients (lost coverage, repeat applications)

sources.note: June 1, 2026 interim final rule narrows medical-frailty exemption; Oregon, California, Pennsylvania say it forces IT rework and adds administrative burden and churn.
New Mexico Medicaid officials: 'more paperwork for everyone', ~88,000 projected to lose coverage, $32.7M initial system-change cost.
CMS March 2026 guidance: two transition options for six-month renewals applying to renewals on/after Dec 31, 2026.
National Council explainer on H.R.1 redetermination changes for behavioral-health providers, including mixed-household renewal-date issues.
Cites Urban Institute projections (up to 3.1M lower enrollment, ~11% procedural) and CBO (~700,000 more uninsured in 2034; $63B).
KFF unwinding data: procedural disenrollment ranged from 96% (NM) to 7% (OR); Arkansas 80%+ procedural.

firsthand_evidence: New Mexico Medicaid leadership described the coming regime as 'more paperwork for everyone' and projected roughly 88,000 residents losing coverage; Oregon's health authority told CMS the June 2026 rule would force it to 'rework and reprogram' IT systems and produce unnecessary churn on and off Medicaid.
key_unknowns: Measured (not projected) disenrollment once six-month renewals start in 2027; how many states choose the all-at-once option; what share of FQHC visits convert to uninsured/self-pay; whether states will accept third-party or provider-attested work/exemption documentation; search budget ran out before Georgia Pathways reporting-failure data could be checked.
technical_unlock: States must publish renewal and work-requirement rules and most have online portals; a patient-facing reminder/document-assembly layer or a health-center-facing renewal-date tracker (built on eligibility data the center already holds) needs no state system access. Direct integration with state eligibility systems would require institutional access.
why_now: H.R.1 (July 2025) hard deadlines: six-month renewals from Dec 31, 2026 and work requirements by Jan 1, 2027; CMS's June 2026 interim final rule changed exemption rules mid-implementation; Nebraska already rolled out in May 2026.
existing_solutions: State eligibility systems and vendors (Deloitte, Gainwell), navigator/assister programs, text-reminder vendors, home-care EVV vendors adding churn modules (e.g., myEZcare per search results), Unite Us/findhelp for social referrals.

title: Referrals and records between independent clinics still move by fax, and one in four practices lacks fax integrated with its EHR
affected_user: Referral coordinators, medical records clerks, and front-desk staff at independent and specialty practices; receiving specialists who cannot find the referral; patients whose records do not arrive before an appointment
job_to_be_done: Send a referral with supporting records to another practice (or receive one) so the patient can be scheduled and seen with the right information
current_process: Print or export from EHR, fax to the other office, phone to confirm receipt, re-fax when lost; receiving staff manually scan faxes and attach them to the right chart; larger systems on Epic use Care Everywhere/TEFCA but small practices on different EHRs fall back to fax
what_fails: Faxes go unanswered or get lost, referrals sit unscheduled, records arrive unindexed; ~70% of hospitals still use fax for some exchange (Univ. of Utah, Apr 2026); roughly half of prior authorization traffic still moves by fax (CMS 'Axe the Fax'); nearly 1 in 4 practices has no fax integrated with EHR/PM (MGMA Mar 2026)
failure_frequency: Daily per practice; no 2026 figure for share of referrals lost or delayed found
cost_of_failure: unknown in dollars; staff time scanning/indexing and phoning, delayed specialist visits, repeated tests
existing_workaround: Cloud e-fax services, staff phone follow-up, patients hand-carrying records or using portals, referral-management vendors, joining a TEFCA QHIN via EHR vendor where available
who_pays_today: Practices (e-fax subscriptions, scanning staff, referral coordinators); EHR vendors (TEFCA onboarding); patients (delays, repeated imaging/labs)

sources.note: University of Utah webinar slide: 70% of hospitals still use fax for some health data exchange.
Cites March 2026 MGMA poll: 73% of practices have digital fax integrated with EHR/PM, nearly 1 in 4 does not; explains why mismatched EHRs make fax the universal denominator for small clinics.
Physicians Practice guide on eliminating fax; references CMS 'Axe the Fax' initiative targeting the roughly half of PA traffic still sent by fax.
TEFCA status 2026: ~500M records exchanged by Feb 2026, over 1B by June 2026; treatment/referral exchange is the most common purpose; participation voluntary.
2026 MIPS PI measure for TEFCA exchange covers all transitions of care and referrals ordered by the clinician.
Referral-vendor commentary on persistent fax-based referral workflows.

firsthand_evidence: No individual clinic-staff complaint surfaced (Reddit threads did not appear in results); the evidence is poll-based: MGMA's March 2026 poll found nearly one in four practices still has fax that is not integrated with its EHR, and a University of Utah April 2026 presentation put hospital fax use at 70%.
key_unknowns: Share of referrals that are lost or require re-send; whether TEFCA's 22,000 connected clinics (vendor-reported, April 2026) include many small independent practices on non-Epic EHRs; what fraction of records requests from patients are delayed; whether the 2026 MIPS TEFCA measure is moving small practices.
technical_unlock: TEFCA QHIN query via EHR vendors is now live at scale (1B+ exchanges), and e-fax APIs plus document OCR/structuring can turn inbound faxes into indexed records; a referral-tracking layer that sits on top of fax for the non-TEFCA long tail is buildable without hospital partnerships.
why_now: TEFCA went from ~10M to 1B+ records exchanged between Jan 2025 and Jun 2026, CMS launched 'Axe the Fax' in 2026, and the 2026 MIPS PI program added a TEFCA exchange measure, so the gap between connected hospitals and fax-bound small practices is widening.
existing_solutions: Epic Care Everywhere, TEFCA QHINs (Epic, eHealth Exchange, Health Gorilla, etc.), Consensus/eFax, Updox, referral-management vendors (Proficient Health, ReferralMD), Kno2, Insight Health (AI referral processing per press release).

title: Hospital and clinic pharmacies spend 20-60 staff hours a week managing drug shortages, which rose for three straight quarters in 2026
affected_user: Hospital pharmacy directors, buyers, and clinical pharmacists; outpatient infusion and oncology clinic pharmacy staff; nurses who must switch products and doses
job_to_be_done: Keep essential drugs (injectables, oncology, anesthesia, ADHD stimulants, GLP-1s) in stock by finding alternative suppliers, therapeutic substitutes, and dose conversions without harming patients
current_process: Daily checks of ASHP/FDA shortage lists and wholesaler availability, calling secondary distributors, rationing and allocation committees, compounding, EHR order-set changes and nursing re-education for each substitution
what_fails: Shortages persist and are rising again (227 active national shortages in Q2 2026, third consecutive quarterly increase, per ASHP/Utah via secondary source); staff time is diverted, substitutions introduce safety risk, and 99% of hospital pharmacists report being affected
failure_frequency: Continuous; ASHP 2024: ~20 hours/week average across hospital sizes, 40 hours at 300+ beds, up to 60-66 hours at the largest; Vizient 2024: 24.2 hours/week per facility vs 10.5 in 2019
cost_of_failure: Roughly 1.5 FTE in large hospitals (ASHP), gray-market premiums, rationed or delayed therapy (Reuters/Yahoo survey of rationing); no 2026 cost figure found
existing_workaround: Dedicated shortage coordinators, secondary wholesalers and gray-market purchases, 503B compounders, therapeutic interchange protocols, manual spreadsheets tracking allocation
who_pays_today: Hospitals and clinics (pharmacy labor, premium pricing); GPOs/wholesalers; patients (delayed or substituted care)

sources.note: ASHP national survey: pharmacy staff spent up to 66 hours/week on shortages in 2024; ~1.5 FTE in large hospitals; ~20 hours/week average.
Secondary summary citing ASHP/University of Utah: 227 active national shortages in Q2 2026, third straight quarterly increase (unverified against ASHP directly).
Vizient survey: average 24.2 staff hours/week on shortages in 2024 vs 10.5 in 2019.
ASHP survey: 99% of hospital pharmacists report experiencing drug shortages.
Survey coverage of hospital pharmacists rationing drugs amid shortages.

firsthand_evidence: ASHP's Michael Ganio is quoted in Becker's saying that in large hospitals managing shortages now requires staff time equivalent to 1.5 full-time employees and that for 300+ bed hospitals it is a full 40-hour job every week.
key_unknowns: Whether ASHP's 2026 survey updates the hours figure (not found); which drug classes drive 2026's increase; what share of shortage work is information-gathering (automatable) vs. clinical substitution decisions; outpatient/independent pharmacy burden vs. hospital (search results were hospital-centric).
technical_unlock: FDA and ASHP shortage lists are public and structured; wholesaler availability data is partly accessible; a tool that watches a facility's formulary against shortage feeds and pre-drafts substitution protocols is feasible, but purchasing integration requires wholesaler access.
why_now: Shortage counts fell to a record low in 2025 then rose for three consecutive quarters into Q2 2026; tariffs and sterile-injectable plant issues are cited as 2026 drivers in secondary sources.
existing_solutions: ASHP/Utah shortage database, FDA shortage list, Vizient and Premier shortage dashboards, wholesaler portals, Bluesight/Kit Check, manual spreadsheets.

title: GLP-1 coverage rules change mid-year and prior authorizations lapse, so patients are denied at the pharmacy counter after their doctor said it was approved
affected_user: Patients prescribed Wegovy/Zepbound/Ozempic; community and chain pharmacists who deliver the denial; prescriber office staff who re-file PAs
job_to_be_done: Fill a GLP-1 prescription that was prescribed and (the patient believed) authorized, at a predictable out-of-pocket cost, month after month
current_process: Prescriber submits PA with BMI/comorbidity/step-therapy documentation; pharmacy runs the claim; on rejection the pharmacist tells the patient to call the plan or prescriber; patient or office appeals, switches drugs, uses manufacturer self-pay programs, or stops
what_fails: Plans drop coverage, add PA, or move drugs to higher tiers between January and summer; Medi-Cal ended Wegovy weight-loss coverage and voided existing PAs on Dec 31, 2025; NPR documents a patient whose physician said the PA was on file but the pharmacy showed Zepbound denied for 'insufficient data'
failure_frequency: unknown; one billing guide attributes most GLP-1 denials to benefit-routing errors, diagnosis mismatches, incomplete PA documentation, or missed formulary changes
cost_of_failure: Patients face list prices of roughly $1,000+/month or ~$499/month manufacturer self-pay programs; prescriber staff time on repeat PAs and appeals; pharmacies lose the fill; no aggregate 2026 figure found
existing_workaround: Manufacturer direct-to-consumer self-pay programs, compounded alternatives, switching between Wegovy/Zepbound/Saxenda based on formulary, appeal-letter templates, Medicare GLP-1 Bridge (from July 1, 2026 per clinic source), employer plan changes
who_pays_today: Patients (self-pay, appeals), prescriber offices (PA staff), PBMs/plans (PA review), manufacturers (DTC discounts), state Medicaid programs

sources.note: NPR: patient told by physician that PA was on file, then told by pharmacist that Zepbound was denied because insurer found insufficient data.
Medi-Cal Rx notice: Wegovy for weight loss alone no longer covered in 2026; prior authorizations approved before the change ended Dec 31, 2025; Zepbound for sleep apnea still needs PA.
Billing-vendor guide: most GLP-1 denials trace to benefit routing, diagnosis mismatch, incomplete PA docs, or missed formulary changes; plans change coverage between January and summer.
GEHA 2026 plan document lists Wegovy and Zepbound as non-preferred with PA required.
Clinic blog describing a Medicare GLP-1 Bridge effective July 1, 2026 under which a prior Part D denial does not disqualify the patient (unverified against CMS).

firsthand_evidence: NPR (June 2026) reports a patient whose doctor assured her the prior authorization was on file, only for the pharmacist to tell her at the counter that Zepbound was denied because the insurer said there was not enough data supporting the request.
key_unknowns: GLP-1 PA denial and reversal rates by payer in 2026; how often PAs lapse without notice to patient or prescriber; pharmacist time per rejected GLP-1 claim (no r/pharmacy threads surfaced); whether the Medicare Bridge and employer coverage cuts are net increasing or decreasing denials; 340B and independent-pharmacy angles were not searched before budget ran out.
technical_unlock: Plan formularies and PA criteria are published (often as PDFs) and change on fixed cycles; an eligibility-and-criteria checker that warns patient and prescriber before the PA expires or the formulary changes is feasible from public documents; real-time benefit check data requires PBM/EHR access.
why_now: State Medicaid programs (e.g., California) and employers cut weight-loss GLP-1 coverage for 2026, Medicare added a GLP-1 bridge program mid-2026, and Aetna reinstated Zepbound on Oct 1, 2026, so coverage status is changing faster than PA cycles.
existing_solutions: CoverMyMeds, Surescripts real-time benefit check, manufacturer savings and DTC programs (LillyDirect, NovoCare), GLP-1 coverage lookup sites (glp1rating, glp1clinics), telehealth weight clinics handling appeals.
